newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian market surge reflects fundamentals.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian market surge reflects fundamentals.

text.p: The strengthening of Indonesia's financial markets since last week's general elections reflected the country's healthy economic fundamentals, economic analysts said on Monday.

The stock market and the Indonesian rupiah regained ground after sliding over past few weeks as campaign fever produced the worst political violence in three decades before voters went to the polls last Thursday.
But investors brushed aside negative factors on Monday to boost their rupiah assets, while the Jakarta Stock Exchange index breached the psychological 700-point barrier.
The ruling Golkar won over 74 percent of the vote in the world's fourth most populous nation.
The Moslem-backed United Development Party (PPP) won 23 percent, while the third party permitted to run, the fragmented Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) scraped home with just over three percent.
Much of the pre-election violence was between supporters of Golkar and the PPP, and analysts are still waiting to see if the PPP accepts the results without further trouble.
The Jakarta stock exchange composite index closed up a marginal 0.53 percent at 699.73 after briefly going through the 700 barrier. Brokers said profit-taking pulled it back.
The rupiah gained further ground to 2,430.5 against the dollar at the Jakarta close after weakening to a low of 2,445.25 on fears of unrest in the midst of the campaign period.
Analysts said the strong showing was not surprising because it had been widely expected investors would return to trade on fundamentals rather than short-term jitters.

"Apart from the election, nothing has really changed in the case of Indonesia. I would say this probably reflects people coming back into the market," Winston Koh, vice president for market research at J.P. Morgan in Singapore, told Reuters.
"I would say it's back to trading more and more on fundamentals," Koh said.
He noted, however, that it was still too early to say if the recovery continue amid fears of possible post-election violence.
Many dealers remained cautious as the PPP will decide on Thursday whether to accept the poll outcome after the party had claimed there were widespread irregularities during the election.
But the economic backdrop remains favourable for Indonesia.
The next key event is the expected re-election of President Suharto -- who turns 76 next Sunday -- in March 1998.

Economic analysts say investors are keenly interested in the succession issue, and will be carefully watching to see who Suharto selects as his vice-presidential running mate -- and potential successor given his age.

Peregrine Securities said in its latest report there were not enough negatives in Indonesian politics to justify staying out of the market, which was supported by robust growth and sound economic management.
"If politics is not a reason to stay out of the market, it follows that it is now time to buy, with the election about to be out of the way," it said.
"The bull story on Indonesia is that Suharto is no older than Deng Xiaoping when he launched China's reform.

"The bear story is that the seemingly complete absence of a succesion mechanism threatens the country with the risk of a vacuum...but an apparently unified army should ensure necessary stability during the post-Suharto transition," the report said.
